title: The Hard Part of Dementia Care Isn't the Dementia Patient—It's the Caregiver Who Gets Dragged Down
dek: The difficulty of dementia care lies not in the patient's condition itself, but in the caregivers who are worn down day after day—care turns wives into nurses, forces a post-90s worker to quit, love is the starting point but not the support, and the system hasn't caught up with these families.
why: This isn't a health科普 for the elderly, but a sociologist's honest fieldwork inside dementia families: no standard answers, only realities you must see before it's too late.
who: Post-80s and post-90s only children, and urbanites whose parents are aging while they've made no eldercare plans; also those who want to understand the real gaps in the care market.

points.h: The care resource gap eventually falls back on every family
points.body: China has 323 million people aged 60 and above, 23% of the total population; 35 million are disabled elderly, yet there are only about 500,000 eldercare workers. The supply gap isn't absorbed by the market or institutions; the pressure mostly falls back on families and individuals. Alzheimer's is not a distant term: reports say China's patient numbers account for nearly 30% of the global total, and the host estimates that on average, one in every 20 Chinese families is affected—for the first generation of only children, this could be the reality their parents are approaching.

points.h: Dementia has no standard symptoms; movies are unreliable
points.body: After interviewing 34 families, Tang Yong most wants to correct the misconception that dementia patients have a uniform image. Society's imagination of dementia comes mostly from movies, neighbors, or hearsay; the professor's incontinence in 'Still Alice' is just one form. He has seen an elderly man who, having been a tailor, still noticed stains on visitors' clothes and taught them to remove them with orange peel; and an elderly woman disabled by a car accident who, when humming 'Liuyang River', was fully focused. Dementia itself covers multiple causes—Alzheimer's, vascular dementia, etc.—and each person's life imprint lingers in different ways; care cannot follow a script.

points.h: The dementia village ideal depends on national care insurance to pay for it
points.body: Most people see the Dutch dementia village Hogeweyk as the ideal answer: residents live like residents, shopping at the supermarket and going to the café, with staff posing as shopkeepers to maintain a normal atmosphere. But the host adds details that expose how hard it is to replicate: the 23 houses built in 2009 cost over €18 million, of which €17.8 million was covered by the government, and residents' fees are also covered by long-term care-related schemes. In contrast, what Tang Yong saw in a low-income U.S. nursing home was the opposite: the elevator had to be locked to prevent dementia patients from wandering off. The same disease, but the difference lies not in philosophy but in the national payment system.

points.h: Love isn't enough; sacrifice drags down the caregiver
points.body: The host captures the caregiver's predicament well: many swing between 'I love my parents very much' and 'I'm about to be dragged down by them.' Tang Yong says care is not one-way help but a relationship; when a spouse has to learn to bathe, feed, and manage emotions, the original equal partnership is overlaid by a nurse-patient relationship. Long-term sacrifice is not a beautifiable devotion: twenty years ago in Guangzhou, he interviewed a daughter who, after caring for her disabled father, divorced and fell into severe depression; the book also features a post-90s caregiver forced to quit due to caregiving pressure. Love is the starting point, but without external resources and community support, caregivers themselves become patients.

points.h: The more you see, the less certain you are about eldercare
points.body: Having studied eldercare for years, Tang Yong himself has no clear plan for his own parents' care. He is a first-generation only child; his parents are both 75 this year, but the more cases he sees, the less certain he feels; his research assistant even said after each interview that the more families she saw, the less she knew how to arrange care for her own parents. Multi-child families have friction too: who does more, who pays less, or someone's rough caregiving causes bedsores; only-child families lack shared manpower, and one person who moved his parents to Shenzhen found rent, medical costs, and nanny fees stacking up faster than retirement wages rose. The ideal model cannot be designed by a single child alone.

points.h: The pain of dementia care is losing someone every day
points.body: The biggest difference between dementia care and disability care is that caregivers must repeatedly accept loss. While volunteering in Seattle, Tang Yong observed an elderly man who initially could draw blue lines on wet watercolor paper, but weeks later only dared to praise others, afraid to put brush to paper; another elderly man's husband reported new losses weekly: his wife couldn't recognize their daughter's newborn grandson, not knowing where this child came from. This daily, irreversible downward slide is more draining on caregivers than physical disability. The long duration of care is not repetitive hardship but facing a small farewell every day.

points.h: Long-term care insurance has arrived, but it doesn't cover all elderly
points.body: Long-term care insurance was piloted in Qingdao and Shanghai in 2016, and by around 2025 it had expanded to about 90 cities; the official pace is to move toward universal coverage in the next two to three years. But Tang Yong reminds that long-term care insurance doesn't hand out cash to every elderly person; instead, through unified assessment, it mainly covers those with moderate to severe disability, paying for home care, meal delivery, and other services; those with mild disability may not qualify. The hardest part is also cultural: sending parents to a nursing home is often equated with filial impiety in China, and elderly people, like the grandfather in the interview, feel their hair would fall out within a month of staying. Tang Yong's judgment is that as younger generations age, the proportion choosing institutional care will rise, but the institutional gap won't disappear on its own.

So I think care should still be a kind of relationship. In this relationship, I think both the caregiver and the care recipient undergo huge changes in identity, emotions, and even the pace of their lives.
It's like going down a slide—you're on a downward path. So at that moment, I think this kind of care is indeed long and drawn-out.
I think although love is a very important foundation, it shouldn't be the only condition for care. It still requires external resources, including social support, and so on.

Although the more I see and the more cases I encounter, it doesn't mean I have a very complete or perfect plan for my parents' future care. Precisely because I've seen so many different stories, it actually leaves me with more confusion.
